metadata.summary: This international consensus addresses the evaluation and management of sellar or parasellar lesions discovered unexpectedly on imaging performed for another reason. It covers specialist referral, dedicated imaging, hormone and visual assessment, surveillance, and indications for surgery across pituitary adenomas, cystic lesions and empty sella. Management is tailored to lesion and patient characteristics, with specific consideration of genetic syndromes, children and adolescents, older people, and pregnancy.

care_settings: multidisciplinary pituitary tumour centre of excellence
target_population: patients with incidentally discovered sellar or parasellar lesions
patients with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1

toxicities.incidence: In patients undergoing cyst drainage: 0–9%; in patients undergoing complete cyst removal: 19–69%.

prevention: Avoid postoperative cerebrospinal fluid leakage; cyst closure might be necessary.

therapies_index.name: observation
approved_indications: MicroNFPAs are generally observed rather than resected.
Observation may be considered for patients >65 years old, or patients of any age with poor functional status, when an adenoma touches the optic chiasm but vision remains intact.
Close observation may be suitable for frail patients with asymptomatic macroadenomas.
Small arachnoid cysts (<10 mm) and larger asymptomatic arachnoid cysts (≥10 mm) may be observed.

Observation may be reasonable for frail patients with stable craniopharyngiomas <10 mm if there are no central signs or symptoms of mass effect, or for patients ≥65 years old or frail patients with large craniopharyngiomas if vision remains intact.
monitoring: Use serial pituitary MRI at intervals determined by lesion size, growth, proximity to the optic chiasm and clinical features.
Reassess pituitary hormones and visual function as indicated by lesion characteristics or new symptoms.

therapies_index.name: surgical resection
approved_indications: Hypersecreting pituitary adenomas are managed surgically according to the relevant current guidelines.
Surgery is recommended when an adenoma causes visual compromise, cranial neuropathy or another neurological deficit.

After assessment at a pituitary tumour centre of excellence, surgery is recommended for an adenoma abutting the optic chiasm, subject to the stated allowance for observation in patients >65 years old or those with poor functional status and intact vision.
Surgery is recommended for enlarging cystic lesions associated with visual or hormonal dysfunction.
Resection is recommended for enlarging craniopharyngiomas and large craniopharyngiomas (≥10 mm), with the stated allowance for observation in older or frail patients whose vision is intact.
key_toxicities: New postoperative pituitary deficits can occur; recovery of pre-existing deficits is not assured.

therapies_index.name: cyst drainage
approved_indications: Described as a surgical approach for Rathke cleft cysts when resection is considered.
key_toxicities: New AVP-D occurred in 0–9% of patients after cyst drainage.

therapies_index.name: complete cyst removal
approved_indications: Described as a surgical approach for Rathke cleft cysts when resection is considered.
key_toxicities: New AVP-D occurred in 19–69% of patients after complete cyst removal.

therapies_index.name: cyst closure
approved_indications: Closure may be needed during Rathke cleft cyst surgery to avoid a postoperative cerebrospinal fluid leak.

therapies_index.name: surgical decompression
approved_indications: May relieve symptoms caused by craniopharyngioma mass effects.
key_toxicities: The guideline notes treatment-associated morbidity from surgery for craniopharyngiomas without specifying an event or rate.

therapies_index.name: gross total resection
approved_indications: Can achieve remission in craniopharyngioma when complete removal is safe.
key_toxicities: The guideline notes treatment-associated morbidity from surgery for craniopharyngiomas without specifying an event or rate.

therapies_index.name: subtotal resection
approved_indications: For craniopharyngioma, subtotal removal followed by radiation may provide long-term control comparable to gross total resection.
therapies_index.administration: Followed by radiation in the treatment approach described.
key_toxicities: The guideline notes treatment-associated morbidity from surgery for craniopharyngiomas without specifying an event or rate.

therapies_index.name: radiation therapy
approved_indications: May follow subtotal resection of craniopharyngioma for long-term control.
Medication and/or radiation is recommended after resection of an enlarging or large craniopharyngioma (≥10 mm) if gross total resection is not achieved.
key_toxicities: The guideline notes treatment-associated morbidity from radiation for craniopharyngiomas without specifying an event or rate.

therapies_index.name: trial of medical therapy
approved_indications: Presented as an option for consideration at a pituitary tumour centre of excellence when the nature of an incidental sellar or parasellar lesion remains uncertain after dedicated imaging.

therapies_index.name: medication
approved_indications: Medication and/or radiation is recommended after resection of an enlarging or large craniopharyngioma (≥10 mm) if gross total resection is not achieved; no medication is specified.

therapies_index.name: anti-headache medication
approved_indications: Discussed as treatment whose failure to control severe headache can prompt consideration of surgical risks and benefits for an adenoma or a small RCC (<10 mm).

recommendations.statement: When feasible, consult an endocrinologist after a pituitary incidentaloma is first identified to establish the diagnosis, arrange hormonal assessment and detailed imaging, and plan the timing of subsequent evaluations.
recommendations.source_heading: When is an endocrinology consultation warranted?

recommendations.statement: Consult an endocrinologist and, when appropriate, a neurosurgeon if a pituitary incidentaloma has any feature suggesting that early intervention might be needed.
recommendations.context: R2; features include maximal adenoma diameter ≥10 mm or cavernous sinus invasion; 15–20% growth in maximum diameter relative to prior imaging; a visual field deficit or a lesion abutting or near the optic chiasm or occupying the suprasellar space; ophthalmoplegia or severe headache; findings suggestive of hypopituitarism or hormone hypersecretion; or planned pregnancy or detection during pregnancy.
recommendations.rationale: These findings might indicate a need for intervention at an early stage.
recommendations.source_heading: When is an endocrinology consultation warranted?

recommendations.statement: For most patients whose pituitary or sellar lesion was found incidentally on other brain imaging, obtain an MRI using pituitary-dedicated sequences.
recommendations.context: R3; examples of initial imaging include CT, brain MRI and 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) PET-CT.
recommendations.rationale: Initial imaging might not characterize a sellar or parasellar finding adequately.
recommendations.source_heading: When is dedicated pituitary imaging warranted? At diagnosis.

recommendations.statement: Use gadolinium enhancement for pituitary MRI unless it is contraindicated.
recommendations.context: R4; characterization of an incidental pituitary lesion
recommendations.source_heading: When is dedicated pituitary imaging warranted? At diagnosis.

recommendations.statement: Where feasible, use a standardized MRI protocol comprising coronal and sagittal T1-weighted spin echo images before and after gadolinium, together with coronal T2-weighted fast (turbo) spin echo images; use a slice thickness ≤3 mm.
recommendations.rationale: A consistent protocol helps identify the lesion and compare later scans.
recommendations.source_heading: When is dedicated pituitary imaging warranted? At diagnosis.

recommendations.statement: Consider foregoing dedicated pituitary imaging when the available images already contain enough information to support a possible diagnosis.
recommendations.source_heading: When is dedicated pituitary imaging warranted? At diagnosis.

recommendations.statement: Individualize the timing of the first surveillance scan. Without new or worsening signs or symptoms, acceptable intervals are 2–3 years for microadenomas, 1 year for macroadenomas ≥5 mm from the optic chiasm, and 6–12 months for macroadenomas <5 mm from the optic chiasm if surgery is not undertaken.
recommendations.context: R7; first imaging procedure after diagnosis
recommendations.source_heading: Intervals for regular surveillance.

recommendations.statement: When choosing subsequent imaging intervals, consider the patient's age; adenoma growth rate and direction after the first repeat MRI; whether the lesion is solid or cystic; its T2-weighted signal intensity; and pituitary stalk deviation.
recommendations.rationale: These characteristics might help assess the likelihood of progression.
recommendations.source_heading: Intervals for regular surveillance.

recommendations.statement: Repeat MRI every 1–2 years for slowly enlarging macroadenomas and for stable macroadenomas <5 mm from the optic chiasm. An enlarging or invasive macroadenoma, including one extending into the cavernous sinus, might need imaging at shorter intervals and consideration of surgery.
recommendations.source_heading: Intervals for regular surveillance.

recommendations.statement: For stable macroadenomas ≥5 mm from the optic chiasm, repeat MRI every 2–3 years.
recommendations.source_heading: Intervals for regular surveillance.

recommendations.statement: If a microadenoma <5 mm remains stable on MRI repeated 2–3 years after the initial MRI and no signs or symptoms are new or worsening, reassess whether regular imaging remains necessary, particularly when life expectancy or functional status is reduced or surgery is contraindicated.
recommendations.context: R11; there was no consensus on when imaging should stop. Some Consensus Group members considered another scan after 5 years according to clinical circumstances, for example in patients <40 years of age.
recommendations.rationale: Microadenomas have a relatively low likelihood of clinically important growth.
recommendations.source_heading: Discontinuing surveillance imaging.

recommendations.statement: At initial presentation, assess pituitary hormones in every patient with an incidental sellar lesion, regardless of its size, and in patients with incidentally identified empty sella.
recommendations.rationale: Symptoms at presentation do not reliably indicate whether pituitary dysfunction is present.
recommendations.source_heading: When is pituitary function testing warranted? At diagnosis.

recommendations.statement: In all patients with an incidentally detected pituitary adenoma, measure prolactin and insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF1) to screen for prolactin and growth hormone hypersecretion; screen for hypercortisolism when clinically indicated.
recommendations.rationale: Hormone hypersecretion can have subtle clinical manifestations; screening for hypercortisolism without clinical indications has a high false-positive rate.
recommendations.source_heading: When is pituitary function testing warranted? At diagnosis.

recommendations.statement: Screen all patients with sellar lesions for hypopituitarism at baseline by measuring free thyroxine (T4), thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), morning cortisol, ACTH, luteinizing hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and IGF1. Measure testosterone in men and oestradiol in women when needed. Perform dynamic hypothalamus–pituitary–adrenal axis testing if morning cortisol suggests hypocortisolism; selected patients might need dynamic testing for growth hormone deficiency after other pituitary hormone deficiencies have been corrected. Gonadal hormone tests are unnecessary for premenopausal women with regular menses.
recommendations.rationale: Hormonal deficits can occur across lesion sizes and need not correspond to symptoms.
recommendations.source_heading: When is pituitary function testing warranted? At diagnosis.

recommendations.statement: For patients with established hormone hypersecretion or hypopituitarism, follow the current guidelines applicable to those conditions.
recommendations.source_heading: When is pituitary function testing warranted? During follow-up.

recommendations.statement: Repeat pituitary hormone assessment for all patients with microadenoma and macroadenomas at 1–2 years, or sooner if new clinical symptoms arise.
recommendations.rationale: New hypopituitarism is uncommon but can arise even without simultaneous lesion growth.
recommendations.source_heading: When is pituitary function testing warranted? During follow-up.

recommendations.statement: Reassess pituitary hormones when a microadenoma or macroadenoma enlarges.
recommendations.source_heading: When is pituitary function testing warranted? During follow-up.

recommendations.statement: Arrange ophthalmological consultation and visual field testing if a patient reports visual symptoms or the lesion touches the optic nerves or chiasm, irrespective of lesion size.
recommendations.source_heading: When is ophthalmological evaluation warranted? At diagnosis.

recommendations.statement: Consider visual field testing for incidentalomas ≥10 mm in diameter and for sellar lesions <10 mm in diameter situated close to the optic chiasm (<3–5 mm).
recommendations.source_heading: When is ophthalmological evaluation warranted? At diagnosis.

recommendations.statement: If surgery is not undertaken in a patient with suprasellar extension, repeat visual field testing after 6 months.
recommendations.source_heading: When is ophthalmological evaluation warranted? At follow-up.

recommendations.statement: Repeat visual field testing at 1–2 years in every patient with a macroadenoma.
recommendations.rationale: Baseline growth and distance from the optic chiasm do not invariably predict later visual deterioration.
recommendations.source_heading: When is ophthalmological evaluation warranted? At follow-up.

recommendations.statement: For macroadenomas that do not compress the optic chiasm and are monitored with annual MRI, perform visual field testing at 6–12 months.
recommendations.rationale: Interim visual testing might identify early growth before the next MRI.
recommendations.source_heading: When is ophthalmological evaluation warranted? At follow-up.

recommendations.statement: Refer patients whose visual field testing is abnormal for neuro-ophthalmological evaluation.
recommendations.source_heading: When is ophthalmological evaluation warranted? At follow-up.

recommendations.statement: Manage incidentally identified hormone-hypersecreting pituitary adenomas surgically in accordance with current guidelines.
recommendations.source_heading: When is surgical resection indicated for incidental NFPAs?

recommendations.statement: Perform surgery when an adenoma causes visual impairment, cranial neuropathy or another neurological deficit.
recommendations.source_heading: When is surgical resection indicated for incidental NFPAs?

recommendations.statement: After assessment at a pituitary tumour centre of excellence, operate on patients whose adenoma touches the optic chiasm. Observation can instead be considered if vision is intact and the patient is >65 years old or has poor functional status at any age.
recommendations.source_heading: When is surgical resection indicated for incidental NFPAs?

recommendations.statement: When an adenoma is ≥5 mm from the optic chiasm, individualize management according to mass size and patient age. A surgical consultation could be considered for young patients with macroadenomas, for serial MRI evidence of growth or cavernous sinus invasion, and for women planning pregnancy.
recommendations.source_heading: When is surgical resection indicated for incidental NFPAs?

recommendations.statement: Suggest surgery for most patients whose pituitary adenoma apoplexy causes severe and/or progressive vision loss or a reduced level of consciousness.
recommendations.source_heading: When is surgical resection indicated for incidental NFPAs?

recommendations.statement: For severe headache that persists despite anti-headache medication, assess surgical risks and benefits after multidisciplinary evaluation that includes an expert neurologist.
recommendations.source_heading: When is surgical resection indicated for incidental NFPAs?

recommendations.statement: For an asymptomatic macroadenoma, weigh patient age and functional status when choosing surgery or observation. Close monitoring for growth might suit a frail patient; if no clinical factor determines the choice, take the patient's preference into account.
recommendations.source_heading: When is surgical resection indicated for incidental NFPAs?

recommendations.statement: Consider surgery for a macroadenoma that enlarges progressively, particularly near the optic chiasm, or when hypopituitarism newly develops; do not assume that pituitary deficits will resolve after surgery.
recommendations.source_heading: When is surgical resection indicated for incidental NFPAs?

recommendations.statement: For an incidental cystic sellar lesion, undertake detailed MRI and hormonal evaluation to establish the differential diagnosis.
recommendations.rationale: Distinguishing cystic lesion types informs subsequent management.
recommendations.source_heading: When is surgical resection indicated for cystic sellar incidentalomas?

recommendations.statement: Have a multidisciplinary team discuss the risks and benefits of surgery for symptomatic cystic adenomas, especially with severe medication-refractory headache or a large cystic lesion accompanied by pituitary apoplexy.
recommendations.source_heading: When is surgical resection indicated for cystic sellar incidentalomas?

recommendations.statement: Monitor small, asymptomatic RCCs (<10 mm) with serial pituitary MRI, choosing the frequency according to clinical features as for pituitary adenomas.
recommendations.source_heading: When is surgical resection indicated for cystic sellar incidentalomas?

recommendations.statement: For a small RCC (<10 mm) with severe headache unresponsive to anti-headache medication, consider surgical risks and benefits following multidisciplinary assessment that includes an expert neurologist.
recommendations.source_heading: When is surgical resection indicated for cystic sellar incidentalomas?

recommendations.statement: Operate on enlarging cystic lesions accompanied by visual and/or hormonal dysfunction.
recommendations.source_heading: When is surgical resection indicated for cystic sellar incidentalomas?

recommendations.statement: Observe small arachnoid cysts (<10 mm) and larger arachnoid cysts (≥10 mm) that are asymptomatic.
recommendations.rationale: Symptoms and enlargement are uncommon in observed arachnoid cysts.
recommendations.source_heading: When is surgical resection indicated for cystic sellar incidentalomas?

recommendations.statement: For a stable, small craniopharyngioma (<10 mm), have a multidisciplinary team discuss observation versus surgery using the available evidence. In a patient suitable for surgery, expert neurosurgical resection might permit complete, safe removal and pathological confirmation; for a frail patient without central signs or symptoms of mass effect, observation might be reasonable.
recommendations.source_heading: When is surgical resection indicated for cystic sellar incidentalomas?

recommendations.statement: Resect enlarging and large craniopharyngiomas (≥10 mm), followed by medication and/or radiation if gross total resection cannot be achieved. Observation might be reasonable when vision remains intact in patients ≥65 years old or in frail patients.
recommendations.source_heading: When is surgical resection indicated for cystic sellar incidentalomas?

artifacts.title: Fig. 1 | Assessment of an incidentally discovered pituitary adenoma managed conservatively
artifacts.description: Step 1: Identify an incidental pituitary adenoma and assess pituitary function at presentation; obtain dedicated pituitary MRI in most cases when the initial examination was brain MRI or CT. Assess vision, including visual fields when symptoms are present or the lesion abuts the optic chiasm. Step 2: Separate microadenomas from macroadenomas and assess growth, symptoms, suprasellar extension and distance from the optic chiasm. Step 3: For a microadenoma without a reason for earlier reassessment, repeat MRI after 2–3 years; if a lesion <5 mm remains stable, reconsider whether imaging should continue. Step 4: For a macroadenoma ≥5 mm from the optic chiasm, repeat MRI after 1 year; for one <5 mm from the chiasm, repeat it after 6–12 months if surgery has not been undertaken. Subsequent imaging intervals depend on stability, growth and proximity to the chiasm, with the figure showing intervals of every 1–2 years or every 2–3 years in relevant branches. Step 5: Consider interval visual-field assessment for macroadenomas and microadenomas <5 mm from the optic chiasm, and reassess the need for continuing surveillance in stable lesions. The figure also identifies cranial neuropathy, solid versus cystic appearance, high-intensity T2 and pituitary stalk deviation as considerations. Patients with documented hormone excess or hypopituitarism are followed under the relevant guidelines; assessment of cystic or other sellar and parasellar masses is individualized.
artifacts.summary: The flowchart links baseline pituitary, imaging and visual assessments to follow-up decisions based chiefly on adenoma size, behaviour and optic-chiasm proximity.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It helps select surveillance intervals while highlighting circumstances that warrant closer visual assessment or reconsideration of continued imaging.

artifacts.title: Fig. 2 | Baseline imaging assessment of an incidental sellar or parasellar lesion
artifacts.source_heading: Factors influencing consultation with an expert neuroradiologist
artifacts.description: Step 1: After an incidental sellar or parasellar lesion is identified, refer to an endocrinologist and review current and previous imaging, clinical circumstances and the pituitary laboratory profile. Step 2: If imaging together with the available clinical and laboratory findings supports a specific diagnosis, manage and arrange imaging follow-up according to relevant guidance or clinical practice, with referral to a PTCOE when indicated. Step 3: If the diagnosis remains uncertain, obtain dedicated pituitary MRI using coronal and sagittal T1 spin echo before and after Gad and coronal T2 fast spin echo. Step 4: Reassess whether the additional findings establish a diagnosis; if they do, follow the diagnosis-specific management route. If uncertainty persists, refer to a PTCOE to consider further imaging, initial surveillance, surgery or a trial of medical therapy.
artifacts.summary: The flowchart directs baseline evaluation according to whether existing assessment or dedicated imaging can establish the nature of the lesion.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It identifies when specialist review is appropriate rather than committing to surveillance or intervention while the diagnosis remains uncertain.

artifacts.title: Box 3 | Future research directions

rows: Undertake prospective follow-up lasting >10–15 years, particularly for patients 40–65 years old, to examine adenoma growth, endocrine changes and overall health effects.
Determine demographic and radiomics-based predictors of sustained adenoma growth and newly developing hormone excess.
Standardize MRI reporting of adenoma volume, optic-chiasm distance in millimetres and modified Knosp classification.
Establish how to distinguish an ‘adenoma’ or ‘likely adenoma’ from heterogeneous enhancement or probable artefact in smaller lesions (<5 mm).
Assess the costs and benefits of frequent clinical review, biochemical testing and imaging.
Investigate whether advanced analytics, including machine learning, improve decisions, imaging interpretation and individualized recommendations.
Study mental health effects of prolonged monitoring, possible hormonal dysfunction and the psychological burden of an asymptomatic monitored condition, particularly in patients <65 years old.
Improve management and monitoring for patients <65 years old, especially young adults and women planning pregnancy.
Define approaches to incidental craniopharyngiomas <10 mm, including possible early targeted therapy for papillary craniopharyngiomas.

artifacts.description: These items are proposed subjects for future investigation, not established management recommendations.
artifacts.summary: The checklist identifies evidence gaps concerning long-term outcomes, risk prediction, imaging, costs, psychological effects and management in selected populations.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It clarifies where current decisions still rely on limited evidence and where further study may change practice.

special_populations.population: Patients with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1
special_populations.considerations: The guideline identifies this group as requiring individualized assessment by an expert multidisciplinary team but provides no further population-specific management details.
Incidental pituitary lesions in children and adolescents call for an individualized approach involving an expert multidisciplinary team.
Age should be considered alongside comorbidities, frailty and functional status rather than used alone to determine management.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: For patients >65 years old with an adenoma abutting the optic chiasm but intact visual function, observation can be considered after evaluation at a pituitary tumour centre of excellence. For patients ≥65 years old with an enlarging or large craniopharyngioma (≥10 mm), observation might be reasonable if vision is intact.

special_populations.population: Frail patients or patients with poor functional status
special_populations.considerations: Functional status and surgical suitability affect the balance between intervention and surveillance. Reduced life expectancy, poor functional status or a contraindication to surgery also bear on whether continued imaging is useful.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Observation can be considered for an adenoma abutting the optic chiasm when visual function is intact despite poor functional status. Close observation might suit frail patients with asymptomatic macroadenomas. For small (<10 mm) stable craniopharyngiomas, observation might be reasonable without central signs or symptoms of mass effect; observation might also be reasonable for enlarging or large craniopharyngiomas (≥10 mm) if vision is intact. For stable microadenomas <5 mm, the need for regular imaging should be reassessed after repeat MRI at 2–3 years, especially when life expectancy is reduced, functional status is poor or surgery is contraindicated.

special_populations.considerations: A desire for pregnancy is a feature warranting endocrinology consultation and, when appropriate, neurosurgical consultation. Fertility goals should inform individualized decisions.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Surgical consultation could be considered for a macroadenoma when pregnancy is desired. For a woman of childbearing age with a large microadenoma or small macroadenoma, surgery or close observation until growth is documented could be appropriate, especially if fertility is desired.

special_populations.considerations: An incidentaloma diagnosed during pregnancy warrants endocrinology consultation and, when appropriate, neurosurgical consultation. Management should be tailored to the patient and lesion by an expert multidisciplinary team.

The guideline identifies young adults as a group for whom management and surveillance need further study. Some Consensus Group members considered additional imaging after another 5 years for selected patients <40 years of age with stable small microadenomas; the group did not agree on when imaging should stop.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Surgical consultation could be considered for young patients with macroadenomas. For a small (<10 mm) stable craniopharyngioma in a patient who is a good surgical candidate, surgery by an expert neurosurgeon might allow safe complete resection and pathological confirmation.

conditions.name: pituitary incidentaloma
conditions.description: An unexpected sellar or parasellar finding identified on imaging obtained for a reason other than suspected pituitary disease. It can represent an adenoma, a cystic lesion, empty sella or another sellar or parasellar process.
conditions.epidemiology: A pooled analysis of imaging studies reported pituitary incidentalomas on MRI at a frequency of 3.4%, although study populations and methods differed. Across 18 clinical studies involving >2,000 patients, approximately 43% of incidental pituitary adenomas were macroadenomas. In a systematic review of 11 studies, growth occurred in 3.3 (95% CI 2.1–4.5) per 100 person-years of microadenomas and 12.5 (95% CI 7.9–17.2) per 100 person-years of macroadenomas.
conditions.clinical_presentation: The imaging study may have been prompted by headache, trauma, cerebrovascular symptoms, ear complaints, cognitive changes or visual disturbances. Previously unrecognized hormone excess, hypopituitarism or local mass effects may nonetheless be present.

subtypes.distinguishing_features: The most frequently diagnosed incidentally found lesion.

subtypes.distinguishing_features: A cystic lesion that is among the more commonly identified incidental findings.

subtypes.name: empty sella
subtypes.distinguishing_features: An incidental imaging finding for which pituitary function assessment is recommended.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize a sellar or parasellar finding and its relationship to adjacent structures.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For most patients after a lesion is detected on other brain imaging, unless existing images adequately establish a possible diagnosis.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The recommended standardized protocol includes T1-weighted spin echo MRI in coronal and sagittal planes before and after gadolinium and T2-weighted fast (turbo) spin echo MRI in the coronal plane, with slice thickness ≤3 mm.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify hormone hypersecretion or pituitary deficiency.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At initial presentation for every incidental sellar lesion, irrespective of size; repeat assessment depends on the lesion and clinical course.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Symptoms alone do not reliably establish whether pituitary dysfunction is present.

diagnostic_workup.test: ophthalmological consultation and visual field testing
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect visual impairment associated with the lesion.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For visual complaints or a lesion abutting the optic nerves or chiasm, regardless of size; testing is also suggested for incidentalomas ≥10 mm and lesions <10 mm close to the chiasm (<3–5 mm).
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Abnormal visual field results warrant neuro-ophthalmological evaluation.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess calcification or extension into skull-base bone.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When these features could clarify the nature of the mass.

diagnostic_workup.test: pituitary MRI after incidental pituitary PET uptake
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate possible primary sellar pathology.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When increased pituitary uptake is found on PET performed for another indication.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The document notes a high likelihood of identifying sellar pathology, while substantial comorbidity or limited life expectancy may affect the decision to investigate.

follow_up.schedule: Imaging intervals depend on lesion type, size, growth, proximity to the optic chiasm and clinical changes. New or worsening signs or symptoms should prompt imaging regardless of the planned interval.
recommended_tests: visual field testing when clinically indicated
long_term_effects: Lesion enlargement may lead to visual impairment, hormone dysfunction or other mass effects.
Long-term surveillance can impose financial costs and contribute to patient anxiety.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Assessment and surveillance should be individualized to the patient's circumstances and the lesion's characteristics.

conditions.name: microNFPA
conditions.description: A clinically non-functioning pituitary adenoma <10 mm in diameter. These lesions usually have no overt manifestations or secretory activity and have a relatively low likelihood of causing hormone deficits.
conditions.epidemiology: In a cohort of 271 microNFPAs, 8.1% enlarged by a mean of 3.1 mm (SD 1.0) over a median of 29 months (range, 3–154 months). Among the 92% without growth in another analysis of that cohort, 10% shrunk and 25.8% were no longer visible on the last MRI. In the UK NFPA Consortium, approximately 10% of 459 patients with microNFPAs had hypopituitarism; 7.2% had hypogonadism and <2% had hypothyroidism or hypoadrenalism.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Most are found without clear symptoms. Hormonal deficiency is less common than with macroadenomas, but the absence of symptoms does not rule it out.

subtypes.name: microadenomas <5 mm
subtypes.distinguishing_features: In one reported series, none enlarged during follow-up; continued imaging may be reassessed after stability on repeat MRI.

subtypes.name: microadenomas ≥5 mm
subtypes.distinguishing_features: In the same series, 14% enlarged during follow-up.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Confirm and characterize the lesion, measure its size and establish its distance from the optic chiasm.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At diagnosis for most patients when prior imaging does not adequately characterize the lesion.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Size, interval growth, proximity to the chiasm, solid or cystic appearance, T2-weighted signal and pituitary stalk deviation can inform subsequent surveillance.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Screen for prolactin and growth hormone hypersecretion.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At initial assessment of an incidentally discovered pituitary adenoma.

diagnostic_workup.test: free thyroxine (T4), thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), morning cortisol, ACTH, luteinizing hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and IGF1
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Screen for hypopituitarism.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At baseline for a sellar lesion and during follow-up as clinically indicated.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Testosterone in men and oestradiol in women are measured when needed; premenopausal women with regular menses do not require gonadal hormone testing.

diagnostic_workup.test: dynamic testing of the hypothalamus–pituitary–adrenal axis
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate possible hypocortisolism.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: If morning cortisol suggests hypocortisolism.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess for visual effects when the lesion approaches the optic apparatus.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For visual complaints, contact with the optic nerves or chiasm, or a lesion close to the optic chiasm (<3–5 mm).

follow_up.schedule: In the absence of new or worsening symptoms, an acceptable interval for the first repeat MRI is 2–3 years. For lesions <5 mm that remain stable on MRI performed 2–3 years after the initial MRI, reassess whether regular imaging remains necessary; consensus was not reached on when imaging should end. Repeat pituitary hormone evaluation is suggested at 1–2 years or earlier for new symptoms, and is recommended if the lesion enlarges.
recommended_tests: visual field testing when proximity to the optic apparatus or symptoms warrant it
long_term_effects: Growth and newly developing hormone deficiency are possible despite their low frequency.
New hormone deficiency can occur without concurrent lesion growth.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Some Consensus Group members considered another MRI after 5 years before stopping imaging, depending on clinical circumstances, including in patients <40 years of age.

conditions.name: macroNFPA
conditions.description: A clinically non-functioning pituitary adenoma ≥10 mm in diameter. Compared with a microNFPA, it is more likely to have visual field effects or cavernous sinus invasion when identified.
conditions.epidemiology: A meta-analysis of 19 studies involving 1,057 patients with NFPAs found growth in 34% of macroadenomas versus 12% of microadenomas (P <0.01), and apoplexy in 5% versus <1% (P = 0.01). Reported macroadenoma growth incidence was 10–14 events per 100 person-years. Approximately 40–45% increased in diameter or volume within 3–4 years, with an additional 5–10% growing during follow-up for >4 years. In a UK NFPA Consortium cohort, previously intact hormone axes developed biochemical hypoadrenalism in 4.0%, hypogonadism in 4.6% and hypothyroidism in 4.9%, with pituitary failure in up to 2.2% despite stable imaging.
conditions.clinical_presentation: A lesion may remain asymptomatic or cause visual field loss, other neurological effects, hypopituitarism or apoplexy. Visual deficits occur predominantly with macroadenomas rather than microadenomas.

subtypes.name: macroadenomas that are <5 mm from the optic chiasm
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Closer imaging and visual surveillance are considered because of proximity to the optic apparatus.

subtypes.name: macroadenomas that are ≥5 mm away from the optic chiasm
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Stable lesions may be imaged at longer intervals.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess size, growth, optic chiasm proximity and invasion of adjacent structures.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At diagnosis and during surveillance when surgery is not undertaken.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Enlargement, cavernous sinus extension, suprasellar extension and proximity to the optic chiasm affect decisions about surveillance or intervention.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Screen for prolactin and growth hormone hypersecretion.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At baseline for an incidentally discovered pituitary adenoma.

diagnostic_workup.test: free thyroxine (T4), thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), morning cortisol, ACTH, luteinizing hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and IGF1
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect pituitary hormone deficiencies.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At baseline, at 1–2 years or earlier with new symptoms, and when the adenoma enlarges.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Testosterone in men and oestradiol in women are measured when needed.

diagnostic_workup.test: dynamic testing of the hypothalamus–pituitary–adrenal axis
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess possible adrenal insufficiency.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When morning cortisol suggests hypocortisolism.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect or monitor visual dysfunction.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At diagnosis if there are visual complaints or contact with the optic apparatus; testing is also suggested for incidentalomas ≥10 mm and during follow-up of macroadenomas.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Abnormal results warrant assessment by a neuro-ophthalmologist.

prognostic_tools.name: modified Knosp classification
prognostic_tools.interpretation: The document proposes including this classification in standardized MRI reports but does not provide its categories or a scoring method.

follow_up.schedule: Without surgery or new symptoms, acceptable timing for the first repeat MRI is 1 year when the lesion is ≥5 mm from the optic chiasm and 6–12 months when it is <5 mm away. Repeat MRI every 1–2 years is recommended for slowly enlarging lesions or stable lesions <5 mm from the chiasm; for stable lesions ≥5 mm away, the recommended interval is every 2–3 years. Enlarging or invasive lesions may need closer imaging. Repeat hormonal evaluation is suggested at 1–2 years or sooner for new symptoms, and recommended with enlargement. Visual field testing is suggested at 1–2 years; with annual MRI and no chiasmal compression, testing at 6–12 months is suggested.
long_term_effects: Potential outcomes include visual impairment, new or worsening pituitary deficiencies and apoplexy.
Pituitary deficits may develop despite stable lesion size.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Age, functional status, growth, lesion location and patient preference inform decisions between observation and intervention.

conditions.name: hypersecreting pituitary adenomas
conditions.description: Pituitary adenomas with hormone hypersecretion; clinical signs may be subtle or become apparent gradually.
conditions.epidemiology: Among 159 surgically resected incidentalomas in a cited study, 6.9% were prolactin-secreting and 5% were growth hormone-secreting. In another series of 65 patients assessed endocrinologically, the corresponding proportions were 6.2% and 3.1%.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Manifestations depend on the hormone secreted. The document describes previously unrecognized features of acromegaly and reproductive symptoms in patients subsequently found to have macroprolactinomas.

subtypes.name: prolactinomas
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Prolactin-secreting adenomas identified among incidental lesions.

subtypes.name: growth hormone-secreting adenomas
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Adenomas associated with growth hormone excess and potentially unrecognized acromegaly.

subtypes.name: ACTH-secreting adenomas
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Adenomas associated with Cushing disease; testing for hypercortisolism is guided by clinical suspicion.

subtypes.name: TSH-secreting adenomas
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Described as exceedingly rare, particularly when discovered incidentally.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Screen for prolactin hypersecretion.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At presentation for every incidentally discovered pituitary adenoma.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Screen for growth hormone hypersecretion.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At presentation for every incidentally discovered pituitary adenoma.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate suspected Cushing disease.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When clinical features or comorbidities raise suspicion, even without classic signs of hypercortisolism.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The document cautions that these tests have high false-positive rates when used without clinical indications.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize the adenoma and its relationship to surrounding structures.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At initial evaluation when existing imaging is insufficient.

follow_up.schedule: Patients with established hormone hypersecretion are to be followed according to the applicable condition-specific guidelines. If initial testing excludes secretion, further endocrine assessment is not indicated without a clinical reason or signs of an aggressive adenoma during surveillance.
recommended_tests: hormone testing directed by the documented hypersecretion or newly appearing clinical features
pituitary MRI as indicated by lesion characteristics
long_term_effects: A previously silent adenoma can rarely become hormone-secreting; such a change may signal an aggressive pituitary tumour.

conditions.name: Rathke cleft cyst
conditions.description: A cystic sellar lesion that commonly appears incidentally and often remains stable or regresses.
conditions.epidemiology: RCCs account for up to one-third of incidental pituitary lesions in autopsy studies and 19% of non-adenomatous masses found on MRI in a cited study. Among 229 RCCs monitored by serial MRI for a median of 36.6 months, 32% regressed spontaneously. In a separate cohort of 110 RCCs followed for a median of 23 months, 13.6% regressed and 6.4% were no longer detectable.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Many incidentally discovered RCCs are asymptomatic. Larger or symptomatic lesions may be associated with headache, visual effects or pituitary dysfunction.

subtypes.name: small RCCs (<10 mm)
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Asymptomatic lesions are generally considered for imaging surveillance; severe headache resistant to medication can prompt discussion of surgery.

subtypes.name: RCCs >10 mm
subtypes.distinguishing_features: In a cited cohort, maximum cyst diameter >10 mm correlated with hormone dysfunction (P = 0.04).

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize the cyst, distinguish it from other sellar lesions and assess change in size.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At diagnosis and during surveillance according to clinical features.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A waxy internal nodule may be present. Approximately 40% are hypointense on T2-weighted images and hyperintense on T1-weighted images without contrast enhancement; minimal enhancement, a thin wall, location in the pars intermedia and anterior stalk displacement may also occur.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify pituitary dysfunction.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At baseline; monitoring is particularly relevant for cysts >10 mm.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: In a cited series of patients with RCCs not treated surgically, 16% had hypopituitarism at diagnosis, predominantly hypoadrenalism (9.7%).

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess for hypocortisolism.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At baseline.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess visual effects of a cyst near the optic apparatus.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For visual complaints or a lesion abutting the optic nerves or chiasm.

follow_up.schedule: For asymptomatic small RCCs (<10 mm), serial pituitary MRI is suggested at a frequency determined by clinical features, similarly to pituitary adenomas. Pituitary function monitoring is suggested by the reported association between cysts >10 mm and hormone dysfunction.
long_term_effects: Cysts may enlarge, remain stable or regress.
Pituitary hormone dysfunction may occur, particularly with larger cysts.

conditions.name: cystic pituitary adenomas
conditions.description: Pituitary adenomas with a cystic component that may arise after haemorrhage or ischaemic infarction and require distinction from other cystic sellar lesions.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Patients may have headache, visual impairment, hormone excess or other hormonal dysfunction. In a cited surgical series, amenorrhoea and/or oligomenorrhoea, reduced libido and galactorrhoea were reported in 24–47% of patients with cystic pituitary adenomas versus 12.8–34.0% of those with RCC.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish a differential diagnosis for a cystic sellar lesion.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At initial assessment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Described findings include heterogeneous T1-weighted signal, isointense T2-weighted signal, wall enhancement, occasional nodularity, internal septations, eccentric location, invasion or fluid layers associated with earlier haemorrhage.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess hypersecretion and pituitary deficiency and aid the differential diagnosis.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At initial assessment of a cystic sellar lesion.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate possible effects on the optic apparatus.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For visual complaints or contact with the optic nerves or chiasm.

follow_up.schedule: Follow-up is individualized according to patient and lesion characteristics.
long_term_effects: An enlarging cystic lesion may be accompanied by visual or hormonal dysfunction.

conditions.name: arachnoid cysts
conditions.description: Cystic lesions that may result from arachnoid tissue herniating through a defect in the diaphragma sellae.
conditions.epidemiology: They represent 1.4% of sellar lesions. In a cited series of 485 patients with arachnoid cysts identified over a 10-year period, 92.5% of adults and 72.4% of children were asymptomatic. After an average of 31 months, cyst volume was unchanged in 95%, and no previously asymptomatic patients developed symptoms.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Most are asymptomatic. A documented example involved an incidentally identified enlarged, partial empty sella caused by an arachnoid cyst.

subtypes.name: small arachnoid cysts (<10 mm)
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Observation is suggested.

subtypes.name: larger asymptomatic arachnoid cysts (≥10 mm)
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Observation is also suggested while they remain asymptomatic.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize the cyst and assess its size and surrounding anatomy.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During diagnostic evaluation of an incidental sellar lesion.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The lesion is described as isointense to cerebrospinal fluid and without MRI contrast enhancement.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess pituitary function as part of the initial evaluation of an incidental sellar lesion.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At presentation.

follow_up.schedule: Observation is suggested for small cysts (<10 mm) and larger asymptomatic cysts (≥10 mm); the document does not specify a cyst-specific imaging interval.
long_term_effects: In a cited follow-up series of 213 arachnoid cysts over 3.8 years, 5 (2.3%) enlarged and 2 (0.9%) were associated with new or worsening symptoms.

conditions.name: craniopharyngiomas
conditions.description: Sellar or suprasellar tumours that may be found incidentally and can follow a more aggressive course than other cystic sellar lesions.
conditions.epidemiology: They account for 1% of all intracranial tumours and 5–10% of sellar tumours in children.
conditions.clinical_presentation: A lesion may be asymptomatic when detected or cause symptoms through mass effects as it enlarges.

subtypes.name: adamantinomatous tumours
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Described as invariably cystic, confined to the sella and often calcified; calcification, a normal-sized sella and a suprasellar cyst location favour this diagnosis over other cystic lesions.

subtypes.name: papillary tumours
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Often solid or mixed cystic–solid; the document notes that medical treatment could be effective.

subtypes.name: small (<10 mm) stable craniopharyngiomas
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Observation versus surgery is considered through multidisciplinary discussion.

subtypes.name: enlarging and large craniopharyngiomas (≥10 mm)
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The document recommends surgical resection, with further treatment if gross total removal is not achieved.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Define lesion size, cystic or solid composition, growth and relationship to nearby structures.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At diagnosis and during assessment of a stable lesion under observation.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Wall enhancement and T1-weighted hyperintensity can occur; calcification and location help distinguish adamantinomatous tumours.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Differentiate a craniopharyngioma from an RCC.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When the differential diagnosis includes these cystic lesions.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An RCC wall is less likely to enhance.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Help confirm the diagnosis of a craniopharyngioma or another non-pituitary lesion.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When additional assessment is needed to clarify the lesion.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Calcification favours adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma over other cystic lesions.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess endocrine function in a patient with an incidental sellar lesion.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At presentation.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify visual effects of the lesion.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For visual complaints or contact with the optic nerves or chiasm.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Confirm the diagnosis.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: If surgery is undertaken for a small lesion in a suitable surgical candidate.

follow_up.schedule: For a small (<10 mm) stable lesion, observation versus surgery is discussed individually. The document gives no fixed imaging interval. Growth, symptoms, visual function, age and frailty influence subsequent management.
long_term_effects: Lesion growth can produce mass effects.
Both surgery and radiation therapy carry treatment-related morbidity.

conditions.name: empty sella
conditions.description: A sellar imaging finding that may be discovered incidentally; pituitary function cannot be inferred from pituitary volume alone.
conditions.epidemiology: Among 402 patients with primary empty sella in a cited study, 40.5% had at least one deficient hormone axis; among the 289 diagnosed incidentally, the proportion was 29%.
conditions.clinical_presentation: It may be found without suspected pituitary disease. Hormone deficiency was more frequent in patients investigated because pituitary disease was suspected than in those diagnosed incidentally.

subtypes.name: partial empty sella
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The document notes that progression to total empty sella could accompany worsening hormonal function.

subtypes.name: total empty sella
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Hypopituitarism is more likely than with partial empty sella.

subtypes.name: Idiopathic
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Listed as a possible cause of empty sella.

subtypes.name: Secondary pituitary atrophy
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Listed in association with apoplexy, hypophysitis, surgery or radiotherapy.

subtypes.name: Congenital gland hypoplasia
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Listed as a possible cause of empty sella.

subtypes.name: Pseudo-tumour cerebri (idiopathic intracranial hypertension)
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Listed in the differential for empty sella.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect hormone deficiencies or hyperprolactinaemia.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At initial presentation when empty sella is discovered incidentally.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: In a cited cohort, male sex (P = 0.02), clinical suspicion (P <0.001) and traumatic brain injury (P = 0.003) predicted hypopituitarism.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize the sellar finding and distinguish partial from total empty sella.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When dedicated imaging is needed to clarify an incidental finding.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Pituitary volume does not correlate with pituitary function.

long_term_effects: Progression from partial to total empty sella could be associated with hormonal deterioration (P = 0.006).

conditions.name: pituitary apoplexy
conditions.description: A complication that can arise in a pituitary adenoma, sometimes as the first recognized manifestation of an incidental lesion. It may be clinically apparent or detected only on imaging or during surgery.
conditions.epidemiology: A systematic review of 11 studies of pituitary incidentalomas reported an overall apoplexy incidence of 0.6 per 100 person-years. In a meta-analysis of NFPAs, apoplexy occurred in 5% of macroadenomas versus <1% of microadenomas (P = 0.01).
conditions.clinical_presentation: Severe or progressive visual loss or reduced consciousness can accompany clinically significant apoplexy. The document also describes subclinical haemorrhage and notes that head trauma may precipitate apoplexy.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess the pituitary lesion and signs of haemorrhage.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When apoplexy is suspected or an incidental lesion requires characterization.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An imaging finding of earlier subclinical haemorrhage is not equivalent to a presentation with clinical apoplexy.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Determine whether visual function is compromised.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When visual symptoms occur.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess endocrine function associated with the sellar lesion.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During evaluation of an incidental sellar lesion.

long_term_effects: Visual and pituitary hormone dysfunction may accompany symptomatic enlargement or apoplexy.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: The document distinguishes evidence concerning clinical apoplexy from incidental imaging signs of prior subclinical haemorrhage.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with a newly identified incidental sellar or parasellar lesion.
decision_rules: Obtain endocrinology assessment when feasible to establish the diagnosis, assess pituitary function and plan imaging and follow-up.
Base subsequent surveillance or intervention on lesion characteristics, hormonal findings, visual and neurological findings, and the patient's clinical circumstances.
Consider assessment by a multidisciplinary pituitary tumour centre of excellence if lesion-related findings arise or worsen, an intervention is contemplated, or the next management step is uncertain.

recommended_regimens.name: Individualized evaluation and management
recommended_regimens.summary: Use specialist assessment and lesion-specific imaging, endocrine and clinical findings to determine whether observation or intervention is appropriate.

response_assessment.method: Clinical assessment, pituitary MRI and pituitary hormone evaluation as indicated by the lesion and any new findings
response_assessment.interpretation: New or worsening symptoms warrant reassessment rather than waiting for the planned surveillance visit.

supportive_care: Explain the available management options, the purpose of assessment and follow-up, and the value of specialist multidisciplinary care.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The document does not define a single treatment schedule for every incidental lesion.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with an incidentally detected microadenoma without an indication for intervention.
decision_rules: Prefer observation to resection when there are no findings that call for intervention.
Individualize the first repeat MRI; in the absence of new or worsening findings, 2–3 years is an acceptable interval unless the lesion lies near the optic chiasm.
Consider lesion size, growth after the first repeat MRI, proximity to the optic chiasm, imaging characteristics and clinical findings when planning later surveillance.

recommended_regimens.name: Observation with pituitary MRI surveillance
recommended_regimens.summary: Monitor an incidental microadenoma conservatively when its clinical and imaging features do not justify intervention.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: First repeat MRI after 2–3 years in the absence of new or worsening signs or symptoms.

response_assessment.method: Repeat pituitary MRI
response_assessment.interpretation: Assess stability or growth and reconsider the need and interval for further imaging.

response_assessment.timepoint: 1–2 years, or earlier if new clinical symptoms appear
response_assessment.method: Repeat pituitary hormone evaluation
response_assessment.interpretation: New hypopituitarism can occur without concurrent lesion growth.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: More frequent imaging can be considered for the uncommon microadenoma close to the optic chiasm. Patients with documented hormone hypersecretion or hypopituitarism should be followed according to the relevant condition-specific guidelines.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with lesions <5 mm that remain stable on a repeat MRI performed 2–3 years after the initial MRI, without new or worsening signs or symptoms.
decision_rules: Reassess whether regular surveillance imaging remains necessary, particularly when life expectancy is reduced, functional status is poor or surgery is contraindicated.
Do not assume that imaging should stop at a fixed time: the Consensus Group did not agree on a stopping point.

recommended_regimens.name: Reassessment of MRI surveillance
recommended_regimens.summary: Review the need for continued routine imaging after the lesion has remained stable on repeat MRI.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Reassess after the repeat MRI performed 2–3 years after the initial MRI.

alternative_regimens.name: Additional repeat MRI
alternative_regimens.summary: Some Consensus Group members considered a further scan before ending surveillance.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider after another 5 years according to clinical circumstances, for example in patients <40 years of age; this was not a consensus recommendation.

response_assessment.method: Repeat pituitary MRI and review of clinical findings
response_assessment.interpretation: Continued stability without new or worsening findings supports reconsideration of regular imaging, but does not establish a universally agreed time to stop.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Reduced life expectancy, poor functional status and contraindication to surgery weigh particularly strongly in the decision about continued surveillance.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients managed without surgery whose incidental macroadenoma is ≥5 mm from the optic chiasm.
decision_rules: In the absence of new or worsening findings, obtain the first follow-up MRI after 1 year.
For a stable macroadenoma that remains ≥5 mm from the optic chiasm, repeat MRI every 2–3 years.
Shorten the interval and reconsider intervention if the lesion enlarges, becomes invasive or causes new findings.

recommended_regimens.name: Observation with pituitary MRI surveillance
recommended_regimens.summary: Continue imaging surveillance for a stable incidental macroadenoma sufficiently separated from the optic chiasm.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: First repeat MRI after 1 year; subsequently every 2–3 years if stable and ≥5 mm from the optic chiasm.

response_assessment.method: Pituitary MRI
response_assessment.interpretation: Evaluate growth, direction of growth, invasiveness and distance from the optic chiasm to set the next interval.

response_assessment.timepoint: 1–2 years, or earlier if new clinical symptoms appear
response_assessment.method: Pituitary hormone evaluation and visual field testing
response_assessment.interpretation: Hormonal or visual deterioration may call for a change in management even when baseline imaging features were not predictive.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: When annual MRI surveillance is used for a macroadenoma that does not compress the optic chiasm, visual field testing at 6–12 months is suggested to identify possible early deterioration between scans.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients managed without surgery whose incidental macroadenoma is <5 mm from the optic chiasm.
decision_rules: Use a shorter first imaging interval because of the lesion's proximity to the optic chiasm.
For a stable lesion that remains <5 mm from the optic chiasm, repeat MRI every 1–2 years.
Consider closer imaging or surgical assessment if growth, invasion or visual deterioration develops.

recommended_regimens.name: Close observation with pituitary MRI and visual surveillance
recommended_regimens.summary: Monitor a macroadenoma near the optic chiasm more closely when resection is not undertaken.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: First repeat MRI after 6–12 months; subsequently every 1–2 years if stable and <5 mm from the optic chiasm.

response_assessment.method: Pituitary MRI
response_assessment.interpretation: Reassess growth and the relationship of the lesion to the optic chiasm.

response_assessment.method: Visual field testing
response_assessment.interpretation: Assess for visual change during observation.

response_assessment.timepoint: 1–2 years, or earlier if new clinical symptoms appear
response_assessment.method: Pituitary hormone evaluation
response_assessment.interpretation: Identify new pituitary dysfunction, including dysfunction without demonstrated growth.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Suprasellar extension warrants consideration of repeat visual field testing after 6 months if surgery is not performed.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients under observation with a slowly enlarging macroadenoma.
decision_rules: Repeat MRI every 1–2 years for slow enlargement.
Consider shorter imaging intervals and surgical intervention when enlargement is more concerning or the lesion is invasive, including cavernous sinus extension.
Reassess visual function, pituitary function and the lesion's proximity to the optic chiasm when deciding whether observation remains appropriate.
