document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: A pituitary incidentaloma is an unexpected sellar or parasellar finding on imaging obtained for a reason other than suspected pituitary disease. This consensus addresses specialist referral, dedicated imaging, hormonal and visual assessment, surveillance, and indications for surgery across adenomas, cystic lesions and empty sella. It also considers multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1, children and adolescents, older people, and pregnancy. Assessment and management should reflect the individual clinical setting. Consultation with a multidisciplinary pituitary tumour centre of excellence should be considered when lesion-related findings are new or worsening, intervention is contemplated, or the next management step is uncertain.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: Pituitary adenomas are the most frequently identified incidental lesions, followed by Rathke cleft cyst (RCC) and empty sella; vascular, inflammatory, infiltrative and infectious causes also occur. A double incidentaloma is very rare and most often involves growth hormone-secreting and adrenocorticotrophic hormone (ACTH)-secreting adenomas. Pituitary adenomas are usually benign and slow to cause clinical problems; morbidity can arise through hormone excess or effects on nearby structures. Literature sometimes uses ‘NFPA’ and ‘pituitary incidentalomas’ interchangeably, although clinically non-functioning pituitary adenomas (NFPAs) are only one category. MicroNFPAs measure <10 mm, generally lack evident symptoms and secretory activity, seldom cause hormonal deficits, and are usually observed. MacroNFPAs measure ≥10 mm and are more likely to have visual field changes or cavernous sinus invasion when identified. Incidentally found and symptomatic NFPAs may differ. Conservative management of many macroNFPAs has enabled longitudinal study, but evidence for incidentaloma management remains limited. Earlier Pituitary Society statements applied GRADE principles: very-low-quality or low-quality evidence generally supported weak recommendations, whereas medium-quality or high-quality evidence supported strong recommendations. This statement distinguishes stronger ‘recommended’ wording from weaker ‘suggested’ wording; consensus on recommendations labelled R1, R2 and onward was reached by voting. The statement covers epidemiology, natural history, investigation, treatment and referral, distinguishing adenomas from other lesions and microadenomas from macroadenomas. Management should be individualized. New or worsening findings warrant consideration of a multidisciplinary pituitary tumour centre of excellence, particularly when intervention or the appropriate next step is uncertain.

document_sections.heading: Methods
document_sections.content: The Pituitary Society convened four virtual Consensus Group meetings between January and September 2024. Workshop Chairs assigned diagnostic and management topics. Evidence summaries critically assessed English-language PubMed-indexed publications available before January 2024. Searches combined incidentaloma terms with epidemiology, natural history, diagnosis, imaging, surveillance, hormones, hypopituitarism, symptoms, visual field assessment and surgery, across specified lesion types. The Steering Committee reviewed summaries and draft recommendations in four rounds and discussed them virtually. In September 2024, recommendations went to a group of 40 endocrinology and neurosurgery experts from 21 countries. Breakout-group discussions informed revisions, and majority opinion determined the final consensus. Later literature was considered using the same search approach, and all authors approved the manuscript.

document_sections.heading: Epidemiology and natural history
document_sections.content: Estimates of incidentaloma frequency come from autopsy, imaging and population-based studies. Autopsy findings do not technically meet the imaging-based definition of incidentaloma, but indicate lesions that might have been detected during life. In a survey of 33 autopsy studies comprising >19,000 examinations, 2,084 lesions yielded a mean prevalence of 10.7% (range, 1.5–31.1%). Study populations and methods differ substantially. Estimates of natural history are also heterogeneous, limiting their use to set surveillance intervals.

document_sections.heading: Epidemiology
document_sections.content: Among incidentalomas detected on MRI, studies report a pooled frequency of 3.4%, with heterogeneous populations and methods. A meta-analysis of 29 MRI studies involving 38,406 patients estimated 2.7 pituitary neoplasms (95% CI 1.7–4.0) per 1,000 scans. Regional cross-sectional studies place the prevalence of clinically relevant pituitary adenomas at 78–94 cases per 100,000 persons; these studies do not consistently separate incidental diagnoses. Reported standardized incidence rose from 0.59–0.73 cases per 100,000 to 1.6–2.0 cases per 100,000 persons per year over 8–14 years. A pooled assessment of 18 clinical studies with >2,000 patients suggests approximately 43% of incidental pituitary adenomas are macroadenomas, although individual estimates differ widely. Costs also matter: an informal Consensus Group survey placed MRI costs from US$ 175 equivalent in a public hospital to US$ 750 equivalent in a private setting in countries with national health systems, versus more than US$ 5,000 in the USA. A pituitary hormone panel may cost as much as US$ 500 equivalent at a private clinic outside the USA and at least twice that in the USA. Patient-specific decisions about testing can reduce costs to patients and health systems.

document_sections.heading: Box 1 | Pituitary incidentaloma: differential diagnosis
document_sections.content: The differential includes anterior pituitary lesions, such as pituitary adenoma, pituitary hyperplasia and pituitary carcinoma; chordoma or chondrosarcoma, germinoma, hypothalamic glioma, pituicytoma and schwannoma; vascular lesions, including intra-cavernous carotid aneurysm and cavernous arteriovenous malformation; infiltrative disease, including sarcoidosis, amyloidosis, haemochromatosis, Langerhans cell histiocytosis and Erdheim–Chester disease; Rathke cleft cyst, cystic pituitary adenoma, dermoid cyst, epidermoid cyst and arachnoid cyst; and empty sella associated with idiopathic causes, pituitary atrophy, congenital gland hypoplasia or pseudo-tumour cerebri. Inflammatory and infectious possibilities include hypophysitis, bacterial abscess, tuberculosis, fungal infection and syphilis. Other neoplasms include craniopharyngioma, meningioma, metastasis, lymphoma and plasmacytoma. Normal anatomical variation and technical artefact are also possibilities.

document_sections.heading: Natural history
document_sections.content: Conservative observation of incidentally detected NFPAs informs estimates of lesion behaviour. A systematic review of 11 studies reported growth in 3.3 (95% CI 2.1–4.5) per 100 person-years for microadenomas and 12.5 (95% CI 7.9–17.2) for macroadenomas. Reports of stability, enlargement and shrinkage vary because of differences in study design, cohort size, imaging methods, follow-up duration and included pathologies. Consequently, these findings cannot readily determine a single surveillance schedule.

document_sections.heading: Diagnosis
document_sections.content: Headache, trauma, cerebrovascular symptoms, inner-ear dysfunction, cognitive changes and visual problems commonly prompt the imaging on which incidentalomas are discovered. The requesting clinician may be in primary care, internal medicine, neurology, otolaryngology, ophthalmology, emergency care or oncology. Headache can be related to a lesion without pituitary disease having been suspected before imaging. Subsequent imaging, endocrine and clinical evaluation should establish whether surveillance or intervention is needed. Assessment should account for potential mass effects, hormonal dysfunction and loss of vision. An increase of 15–20% in maximum diameter on repeat imaging warrants referral to an endocrinologist or neurosurgeon and close observation, although enlargement alone does not necessarily require intervention. A multidisciplinary approach should be considered when management is uncertain.

document_sections.heading: When is an endocrinology consultation warranted?
document_sections.content: R1 recommends endocrinology consultation, where possible, for a newly discovered incidentaloma to establish the diagnosis, arrange hormonal and detailed imaging assessment, and plan reassessment. R2 recommends endocrinology consultation and, where appropriate, neurosurgical consultation when features suggest possible early intervention: maximum adenoma diameter ≥10 mm or cavernous sinus invasion; growth of 15–20% in maximum diameter against earlier imaging; visual field loss or a lesion abutting or near the optic chiasm or situated suprasellarly; ophthalmoplegia or severe headache; findings suggesting pituitary hormone deficiency or excess; or pregnancy planning or diagnosis during pregnancy.

document_sections.heading: Table 1 | Characteristics of pituitary incidentalomas of different aetiologies
document_sections.content: The table compares selected studies by sample size, participant age and sex, lesion characteristics, hypopituitarism, visual defects, surgery, and growth or recurrence. Across its 2,241 patients, mean age was 53 years, 55% were female and 61% of incidentalomas were macroadenomas. Studies were included when incidentalomas defined the study population or constituted a separately analysed subgroup.

document_sections.heading: Box 2 | Indications for imaging resulting in discovery of incidentalomas in two large single-centre studies (n= 413)
document_sections.content: Reasons for imaging included neurological and other symptoms, injury or illness, and miscellaneous indications such as surveillance of another brain mass, dental X-rays, participation in an MRI study and elective screening. The source studies were retrospective chart reviews, which may limit detail about presentations; reasons for imaging differ across centres and countries.

document_sections.heading: Indications for MRI with pituitary-dedicated sequences
document_sections.content: Initial brain imaging may characterize an incidental sellar or parasellar lesion inadequately. Routine CT is not recommended because its soft-tissue contrast and depiction of adjacent invasion, including cavernous sinus invasion, are inferior to MRI. Imaging acquired for another indication can show the gland only incidentally and may use sections as thick as 5 mm. A standardized pituitary protocol improves lesion identification and comparison with later images. A fine matrix, for example 256 × 256 or greater, and a small field of view of 16–18 cm are favoured. Dedicated MRI should generally use gadolinium, although concern about repeated gadolinium exposure has prompted reconsideration of contrast selection and the need for contrast on later examinations. Complete pre-contrast and post-contrast baseline imaging supports diagnosis and may reduce later imaging. Non-contrast CT may be considered to assess calcification or extension into skull-base bone. Incidental focal pituitary uptake occurs in <1% of patients undergoing whole-body 18F-FDG PET-CT in retrospective series. In a review of 40,967 patients, uptake occurred in 30 (0.073%) after exclusion of known lesions; among 19 subsequently assessed by MRI, 18 had an adenoma and none had metastasis. Two other studies involving 13,145 and 24,007 patients found uptake in 0.8% and 0.13%, respectively, and identified adenomas, metastases, and inflammatory or infiltrative lesions. Reports involving 68Ga-DOTATATE, 68Ga-DOTATOC and 18F-choline are too few for reliable incidence estimates. Dedicated pituitary and surrounding-structure MRI is indicated after incidental PET uptake, given the probability of sellar pathology. Major comorbidity or limited life expectancy warrants discussion of a potentially conservative approach.

document_sections.heading: When is dedicated pituitary imaging warranted?
document_sections.content: At diagnosis, R3 recommends MRI with pituitary-specific sequences for most lesions initially found on other brain imaging, including CT, brain MRI or 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) PET-CT. R4 recommends gadolinium enhancement unless contraindicated. R5 recommends, where feasible, a standardized protocol with coronal and sagittal T1-weighted spin echo images before and after gadolinium and coronal T2-weighted fast (turbo) spin echo images, using sections ≤3 mm. R6 suggests that another dedicated examination may be unnecessary if existing images already support a possible diagnosis.

document_sections.heading: Intervals for regular surveillance.
document_sections.content: R7 recommends individualizing the first repeat image. Without new or worsening findings, acceptable intervals are 2–3 years for microadenomas; 1 year for macroadenomas ≥5 mm from the optic chiasm; and 6–12 months for macroadenomas <5 mm from the chiasm if they are not resected. R8 suggests using age, the rate and direction of growth after the first repeat MRI, solid versus cystic consistency, T2-weighted signal and stalk deviation to decide subsequent intervals. R9 recommends MRI every 1–2 years for slowly enlarging macroadenomas or stable macroadenomas <5 mm from the chiasm; invasive or enlarging lesions may need closer imaging and consideration of surgery. R10 recommends MRI every 2–3 years for stable macroadenomas ≥5 mm from the chiasm.

document_sections.heading: Discontinuing surveillance imaging.
document_sections.content: R11 suggests reassessing routine imaging for a microadenoma <5 mm that remains stable on MRI repeated 2–3 years after baseline, provided no new or worsening symptoms have appeared. This is particularly pertinent with reduced life expectancy, poor functional status or a contraindication to surgery. There was no consensus on when imaging should stop. Some group members considered another scan after 5 years according to circumstances, including age <40 years.

document_sections.heading: Factors influencing intervention versus regular surveillance
document_sections.content: Predictors of enlargement are incompletely defined. Compared with microadenomas, macroadenomas generally grow more quickly and more often become symptomatic through visual field loss, pituitary hormone deficits or apoplexy. Imaging appearance, growth trajectory, proximity to the optic apparatus, endocrine findings and patient circumstances may inform the choice between continued observation and intervention.

document_sections.heading: Adenoma size.
document_sections.content: Larger initial size has been examined as a growth risk factor and is incorporated in a proposed prognostic classification, but growth is not inevitable or linear. A meta-analysis of 19 studies involving 1,057 patients with NFPAs found more growth with macroadenomas than microadenomas (34% versus 12%; P <0.01) and more apoplexy (5% versus <1%; P = 0.01). Reported growth incidence is 10–14 events per 100 person-years for macroadenomas and 2–5 per 100 person-years for microadenomas. Approximately 40–45% of macroadenomas enlarge within 3–4 years, with another 5–10% growing after >4 years. Relative to microadenomas, macroadenomas were associated with fivefold greater apoplexy risk, fourfold greater visual field deficit risk and threefold greater pituitary hormone deficit risk. Nevertheless, most lesions remain stable, and some shrink or disappear. Some studies found first growth only after 24–60 months, with growth possible up to 14 years after diagnosis. In one series of 133 incidental NFPAs and other sellar masses, adenoma growth occurred in 2% at 1 year, 5% at 2 years and 9% at 3 years; no microadenomas <5 mm grew, versus 14% of microadenomas ≥5 mm and 25% of macroadenomas. In another series of 271 microNFPAs, 8% grew over approximately 3 years (range, 3–154 months); baseline size, sex and age did not affect median time to growth. Of the 92% without growth, 10% shrank and 25.8% were absent on the last MRI; shrinkage was more likely below 5 mm. Approximately two-thirds of 177 microadenomas remained stable or became smaller during long-term follow-up. Surgical resection occurred in 20–30% of patients with enlarging macroadenomas, versus <4% without enlargement. Growth of 5.9 mm per year or >3.5 mm overall predicted worsening vision; volumetric growth >10 mm3 per month at 2 years strongly predicted a need for surgery. In a UK cohort of 949 macroNFPAs, cumulative shrinkage probability was 9.6% after 5 years; another study found shrinkage in 20% of 49 patients followed for a mean of 4.9 years, averaging 3.5 ± 1.3 mm.

document_sections.heading: Mass effects.
document_sections.content: Clinically consequential enlargement occurs more often with macroadenomas. In a 42-person cohort in which 88% had macroadenomas, 24% experienced symptomatic enlargement with visual symptoms, panhypopituitarism or apoplexy 4 years after diagnosis. Height ≥15 mm, compared with <15 mm, was associated with greater risk of symptomatic enlargement (P = 0.007), although size did not correlate with likelihood of growth. In 271 microNFPAs, 8.1% enlarged by a mean of 3.1 mm (SD 1.0) over a median of 29 months (range, 3–154 months). Visual deficits are uncommon and occur almost entirely with macroadenomas; a meta-analysis reported visual symptoms at 0.65 per 100 person-years (95% CI 47–0.82) in untreated incidentalomas. Among 197 untreated NFPAs observed for a median of 37 months (95% CI 12–170), 4% developed new or worse pituitary dysfunction. In another series of 50 patients followed for 3 years, approximately 8% with macroadenomas and no patients with microadenomas developed hypopituitarism. Across studies, reported macroadenoma apoplexy rates ranged from 3% over a median of 35 months to 14% over 85 months. Apoplexy can accompany either enlargement or shrinkage; size is one of the few independent predictors. Among 385 surgically treated NFPAs, 75% of which were macroadenomas, silent apoplexy was identified in 13%. Apoplexy is rare in microadenomas, can be an incidentaloma’s first manifestation, may be evident only on imaging or at surgery, and can follow head trauma. A systematic review of 11 studies estimated overall apoplexy incidence at 0.6 per 100 person-years.

document_sections.heading: Adenoma consistency.
document_sections.content: Imaging-based assessment of consistency is difficult. Apparently solid lesions presumed to be NFPAs are more likely to enlarge than cystic lesions. Among 265 unresected incidental lesions, NFPA had greater odds of enlargement than non-pituitary sellar masses, 75% of which were RCCs or other cysts: OR 3.92 (95% CI 1.27–12.07; P = 0.017). Two other studies found enlargement in 20% of presumed solid NFPAs observed for 51 months and 23 months, compared with 5% of presumed RCCs observed for 23–24 months. In a UK macroNFPA cohort, a cystic or haemorrhagic component predicted shrinkage; the reported comparison for purely solid lesions was HR 0.30, 95% CI 0.19–0.48.

document_sections.heading: Intervals for imaging during regular surveillance
document_sections.content: Prior guidance combined size with other clinical features when planning imaging. Aggressive biology in a patient <65 years old may justify closer observation than in an older patient, although independent prognostic factors remain difficult to establish and some studies identified none. Possible predictors of enlargement include distance <1 mm from the chiasm, initial size >15 mm, stalk deviation, hormone deficiency at diagnosis, T1-weighted contrast enhancement and high T2-weighted signal. One study found progression more likely in women >50 years than in women ≤50 years or men; separate studies identified either male or female sex as a growth predictor. Another series did not find age independently predictive of surgery. These associations may aid interval selection despite methodological differences. New or worsening symptoms require imaging irrespective of the scheduled date and reconsideration of intervention.

document_sections.heading: Macroadenomas.
document_sections.content: Earlier practice often used MRI every 6 months during the first 2 years and annually for the next 3–5 years. UK NFPA findings instead showed less growth in the first year than in subsequent years through 5 years. If surgery is not performed, acceptable initial follow-up is 1 year when a macroadenoma lies ≥5 mm from the optic chiasm, or 6 months when it lies <5 mm away. Stable lesions may subsequently be scanned less often, with eventual cessation considered according to patient and tumour characteristics.

document_sections.heading: Microadenomas.
document_sections.content: Because clinically important growth is less likely than for macroadenomas, observational evidence supports first repeat MRI 2–3 years after diagnosis unless the lesion approaches the optic chiasm. Some published reviews propose no surveillance for lesions <5 mm; a more cautious option is to stop after stability on MRI repeated 2–3 years from baseline, although some consensus members favoured one further scan after 5 years according to circumstances. For microadenomas ≥5 mm, one review proposed MRI at 6 months, then yearly if growth occurs, or at 2 years if stable. Rare microadenomas near the chiasm may warrant more frequent imaging.

document_sections.heading: Adenoma growth rate.
document_sections.content: Serial MRI during the first 1–2 years can establish growth rate and guide later intervals. In 197 NFPAs, volumetric growth ≥0.88 cm3 per year between the first and second annual scans predicted worsening visual function; slower growth could justify delaying another MRI. Generally, yearly MRI is warranted for slowly growing macroadenomas and stable macroadenomas <5 mm from the chiasm, compared with every 2–3 years for stable macroadenomas ≥5 mm away.

document_sections.heading: Factors influencing consultation with an expert neuroradiologist
document_sections.content: Interpreting pituitary imaging may require specialist expertise despite an optimized protocol. Normal appearance changes during adolescence, menopause and pregnancy. Cystic or haemorrhagic lesions can be hard to characterize, and subclinical haemorrhage that may resolve can be overinterpreted. Early consultation with an expert pituitary neuroradiologist and the wider centre-of-excellence team is advised when intervention is contemplated or lesion type, consistency or next steps are uncertain.

document_sections.heading: Endocrine evaluation
document_sections.content: Hormonal abnormalities can occur despite an absence of suggestive symptoms or lesion growth. Initial assessment and subsequent reassessment should address secretion and deficiency as appropriate to the lesion and changing clinical findings.

document_sections.heading: When is pituitary function testing warranted?
document_sections.content: At diagnosis, R12 recommends pituitary hormone testing for every incidental sellar lesion, regardless of size, and for incidentally identified empty sella; symptoms do not reliably identify dysfunction. R13 recommends measuring prolactin and insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF1) in every incidental adenoma to screen for prolactin and growth hormone excess, with hypercortisolism screening when clinically warranted. R14 recommends initial deficiency screening in every sellar lesion using free thyroxine (T4), thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), morning cortisol, ACTH, luteinizing hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and IGF1; testosterone in men and oestradiol in women are measured when needed. Suggestive morning cortisol results warrant dynamic hypothalamus–pituitary–adrenal testing. Selected patients may need dynamic growth hormone deficiency assessment after other deficiencies are corrected. Premenopausal women with regular menses need no gonadal hormonal testing. During follow-up, R15 recommends care under the applicable condition-specific guidance for established hormone excess or hypopituitarism. R16 suggests reassessing hormones in all patients with microadenomas or macroadenomas at 1–2 years, or sooner for new symptoms, because deficiency can develop without visible growth. R17 recommends repeat testing for enlarging microadenomas and macroadenomas.

document_sections.heading: Fig. 1 | An algorithm for assessment of an incidentally discovered pituitary adenoma on imaging managed conservatively.
document_sections.content: The algorithm links initial hormonal, pituitary MRI and visual assessment to tumour size, symptoms, growth and distance from the optic chiasm. Most lesions first identified on general brain MRI or CT warrant dedicated pituitary MRI. A stable microadenoma <5 mm may have continued imaging reconsidered after repeat MRI at 2–3-year intervals. For macroadenomas and microadenomas <5 mm from the chiasm, visual field testing can occur between MRI examinations scheduled after 6–12 months. Cystic and other sellar or parasellar lesions require individualized follow-up. Documented hormone excess or deficiency is followed under relevant guidance. Head or sellar CT may help confirm craniopharyngioma, chordoma or another non-pituitary diagnosis.

document_sections.heading: Screening for a functioning pituitary adenoma
document_sections.content: Across pooled case series, prolactinomas accounted for 6–18% of incidentalomas. Among 159 surgically removed incidentalomas, 6.9% secreted prolactin and 5% secreted growth hormone; in a series of 65, the corresponding proportions were 6.2% and 3.1%. Another assessment of 35 incidentalomas found growth hormone secretion in 9%. Of 334 clinically silent adenomas at autopsy, 39.5% stained for prolactin, 13.8% for ACTH and 2% for growth hormone. Among 112 surgically treated patients with acromegaly, 17% were diagnosed following incidental imaging, but retrospective assessment identified acromegaly features in 58% and otolaryngological manifestations in 47%. Symptoms prompting imaging can therefore conceal hormonal disease. Screening for Cushing syndrome without suggestive clinical features is generally not recommended because tests have high false-positive rates and may create unnecessary anxiety. Nevertheless, in 68 incidentaloma patients without overt hypercortisolism, 7.3% met biochemical criteria for Cushing disease and 4.4% had ACTH confirmed in resected tissue; another study diagnosed Cushing disease after surgery in 4.8% of 105 patients without overt hypercortisolism. Whether ACTH-secreting adenomas without overt hypercortisolism increase associated cardiovascular, skeletal or other risks is unknown. Features or comorbidities raising suspicion justify screening even without classic findings. Subtle secretion can progress; initial prolactin and growth hormone axis assessment is therefore appropriate for incidental sellar lesions. After a negative initial assessment, further secretory testing is unnecessary unless clinically indicated or surveillance identifies concerning features. Suggestive screening or new clinical findings warrant condition-specific assessment. Conversion of a silent adenoma to growth hormone or ACTH secretion may indicate aggressive behaviour requiring intervention.

document_sections.heading: Fig. 2 | Baseline imaging evaluation of incidentally detected sellar or parasellar lesions.
document_sections.content: The decision pathway first considers prior and current imaging, clinical circumstances and pituitary laboratory findings. If these establish a diagnosis, management follows applicable guidance; if not, dedicated pituitary MRI is obtained. Continued uncertainty prompts expert assessment at a pituitary tumour centre of excellence, with further imaging, surveillance, surgery or a medical-treatment trial considered. Examples include an RCC in a 25-year-old woman, partial empty sella associated with an arachnoid cyst in a 27-year-old man, an aneurysm in a 70-year-old woman, a macroadenoma in a 62-year-old man, a subsequently biopsied adenoma in a 59-year-old man, and a surgically confirmed chordoma in a 45-year-old woman. Historical images can sometimes reveal the lesion on careful review.

document_sections.heading: Screening for hypopituitarism
document_sections.content: Hypopituitarism has been reported in up to half of patients with incidental lesions of varied causes. Luteinizing hormone and/or FSH, TSH and growth hormone deficits are most common; arginine vasopressin deficiency (AVP-D) is fairly uncommon. Deficits occur less frequently with microadenomas, although rates of new endocrinopathies reported for microadenomas and macroadenomas were not significantly different (0.9 and 2.1 per 100 person-years; P= 0.15). Size and symptoms do not reliably predict later dysfunction. A study of 903 patients with sellar masses found deficiency in ≥1 axis among 31% of 222 incidentaloma patients; macroadenoma (P = 0.002) and male sex (P = 0.006) increased risk, although 71% of incidentalomas were macroadenomas. Among 371 patients with NFPA, deficiency at diagnosis occurred in 37% with macroadenomas and 11% with microadenomas (P <0.001); macroadenoma predicted dysfunction (OR 3.38, 95% CI 1.81–6.29; P <0.001). Still, 3% of 187 patients followed for at least 3 years had deteriorating function without growth. In the UK NFPA Consortium, approximately 10% of 459 microNFPA patients had hypopituitarism: 7.2% had hypogonadism and <2% had hypothyroidism or hypoadrenalism. Among patients with macroNFPA and previously intact axes, new biochemical hypoadrenalism, hypogonadism and hypothyroidism occurred in 4.0%, 4.6% and 4.9%, respectively, and pituitary failure occurred in up to 2.2% despite stable imaging. In a comparison of 269 patients with NFPAs >6 mm, hypopituitarism was more frequent in symptomatic than incidental cases (58.7% versus 27.4%; P <0.0001), but absence of symptoms had a negative predictive value of only 71% and did not usefully determine who needed testing.

document_sections.heading: Screening for pituitary dysfunction in patients with RCC
document_sections.content: Estimates of RCC-associated hypopituitarism vary with the axes and tests assessed. Among 62 of 134 nonsurgically managed RCC patients, 48% of whose lesions were incidental, 16% had hypopituitarism initially, chiefly hypoadrenalism (9.7%). At 37 months, hypopituitarism was less frequent, hyperprolactinaemia had resolved in 5 of 10 patients, and no new deficiencies were detected even with cyst enlargement. Maximum cyst diameter >10 mm correlated with hormonal dysfunction (P = 0.04), supporting monitoring for cysts above that size. Because hypocortisolism was present at diagnosis in 25% of patients with resected RCCs, initial hypothalamus–pituitary–adrenal assessment is indicated.

document_sections.heading: Screening for pituitary dysfunction in patients with empty sella
document_sections.content: Hypopituitarism is much more frequent in clinically suspected than incidentally identified empty sella. Pituitary volume does not correlate with function, although total empty sella carries greater risk than partial empty sella. Among 402 people with primary empty sella, 40.5% had ≥1 deficient axis; the rate was 29% among 289 incidental diagnoses. Clinically suspected versus incidental cases had hypothyroidism in 29.2% versus 2.8%, growth hormone deficiency in 20.4% versus 12.5%, hypogonadism in 50.4% versus 8.5%, and hyperprolactinaemia in 15.7% versus 2.9%. Hypocortisolism rates were 17.7% versus 13.5%, and AVP-D rates were 1.7% versus 0.9%. Male sex (P = 0.02), clinical suspicion (P <0.001) and traumatic brain injury (P = 0.003) predicted hypopituitarism. Change from partial to total empty sella may accompany worsening hormone function (P = 0.006).

document_sections.heading: Clinical evaluation
document_sections.content: An incidentaloma can later cause cranial neuropathy, deficient or excessive hormone secretion, headache, visual field or acuity changes, diplopia and, very rarely, hypothalamic dysregulation or cerebrospinal fluid rhinorrhoea. Possible mechanisms identified are central compression, local inflammation and autonomous secretion. Collaborative multidisciplinary assessment is preferred.

document_sections.heading: Indications for repeat endocrine evaluation
document_sections.content: New pituitary hormone deficiency has been reported at 1.2 to 2.4 per 100 person-years in incidentalomas and, for some macroadenomas, up to 11.9 per 100 patient-years. Reported new deficits accompanying growth vary: ACTH, 0.2–39.0%; growth hormone, 0.2–31.8%; TSH, 0.5–21.4%; and luteinizing hormone and/or FSH, 0.2–19.7%. Pre-existing gonadotropin abnormalities may inflate estimated new gonadotropin deficits; limited dynamic testing may underestimate growth hormone deficiency. ACTH stimulation testing is recommended for most patients whose morning cortisol is inconclusive for adrenal insufficiency. In the UK NFPA Consortium, only two of 459 microNFPA patients developed new deficiencies. In 111 NFPA patients followed for a median of 3.75 years (interquartile range 4.33), approximately 5% developed deficiencies without an association with initial diameter in the <5 mm, 5–10 mm or >10 mm categories. In 194 incidental NFPAs followed for a median of 3 years (interquartile range 2–5), new deficiency was unrelated to size; 10 of 194 (5.2%) developed it despite stable or decreasing mass size. In 35 conservatively managed macroNFPAs observed for a median of 50 months, baseline deficiency was associated with earlier growth during the first 2 years, and all with baseline hypopituitarism had grown by year 5. In the Swedish Pituitary Registry, RCC-related hypopituitarism among 204 cysts <10 mm was 3.3% at 1 year and 7% at 5 years; among 174 cysts ≥10 mm, the respective rates were 20% and 22%. Silent hormone-expressing adenomas can rarely become secreting tumours. A review of 20 patients reported conversion to Cushing disease in 4 silent corticotroph and 4 null cell adenomas, and to acromegaly in 1 silent somatotroph adenoma; median time was 72 months (range 12–276). One series found Cushing disease transformation in 5 of 176 (2.8%) resected corticotroph adenomas over an average of 4.2 years; another reported 3 of 75 (4%) over 7 years. Among 16 transformed silent corticotroph adenomas, median time to transformation was 30 months and 50% changed in 12–24 months. These patients underwent a median of 2.5 surgeries (95% CI 2–4), 81% received radiation and only one-third achieved remission. Reports of silent somatotroph conversion are scarce; such lesions are described as more aggressive and treatment-refractory. Among 17 followed for a mean of 3.9 years, 5 developed higher IGF1 and required another operation or radiotherapy.

document_sections.heading: When is ophthalmological evaluation warranted?
document_sections.content: At diagnosis, R18 recommends ophthalmology consultation and visual field testing for visual complaints or a lesion touching the optic nerves or chiasm, irrespective of size. R19 suggests visual field testing for incidentalomas ≥10 mm and sellar lesions <10 mm that are <3–5 mm from the chiasm. During follow-up, R20 suggests repeat visual fields at 6 months for unresected suprasellar extension; R21 suggests testing at 1–2 years for every macroadenoma because initial growth or chiasmal distance may not predict deterioration; and R22 suggests testing at 6–12 months when a non-compressive macroadenoma is monitored with yearly MRI. R23 recommends neuro-ophthalmology assessment for abnormal visual field results.

document_sections.heading: Indications for surgical management
document_sections.content: Choices between more intensive and conservative management should reflect individual benefits and risks, not age thresholds alone. Comorbidity and frailty can independently affect outcomes. The surgical role for incidentalomas, especially NFPAs, is not well established, and randomized studies have not assessed outcomes. A multidisciplinary team should discuss indications, benefits and risks. A related visual defect, cranial neuropathy, other neurological deficit or cavernous sinus invasion warrants interdisciplinary discussion and consideration of surgery regardless of size, with prolactinomas managed under applicable guidance. In a suitable surgical candidate with newly deficient hormones and progressive growth, specialized-centre surgery may be considered, but postoperative improvement cannot be assumed. For asymptomatic lesions, age, functional status, size, cavernous sinus invasion, surgical risk, reproductive plans and patient preference influence surgery versus observation. Observation may be appropriate for a frail asymptomatic patient even when the chiasm is touched. Conversely, some patients may prefer earlier surgery rather than the cost, repeated visits and anxiety associated with surveillance. A prospective international registry of 97 patients with clinical apoplexy found no surgical advantage over conservative care for vision at 3 months, and no outcome difference for surgery at ≤3 days versus >3 days; adenomas shrank in both groups. Because surgically managed patients were more seriously ill, generalization is difficult. Those results do not apply to the 25% with signs of an earlier subclinical haemorrhage on imaging.

document_sections.heading: When is surgical resection indicated for incidental NFPAs?
document_sections.content: R24 recommends surgery for incidentally discovered hypersecreting adenomas according to existing condition-specific guidance. R25 recommends surgery for adenoma-related visual compromise, cranial neuropathy or another neurological deficit. R26 recommends surgery when an adenoma abuts the chiasm after evaluation in a pituitary tumour centre of excellence, while permitting consideration of observation for patients >65 years old or those of any age with poor functional status and preserved vision. For an adenoma ≥5 mm from the chiasm, R27 suggests individualized decisions by lesion size and age; surgical consultation may be considered in young patients with macroadenomas, with growth on serial MRI or cavernous sinus invasion, or in women planning pregnancy. R28 suggests surgery for most patients whose adenoma apoplexy causes severe and/or progressive vision loss or reduced consciousness. R29 suggests weighing surgery’s risks and benefits for severe headache refractory to anti-headache medication after multidisciplinary assessment including an expert neurologist. R30 suggests considering age and functional status for asymptomatic macroadenomas; close observation may suit frail patients, and preference matters when clinical factors do not decide. R31 suggests considering surgery for progressively enlarging macroadenomas, especially near the chiasm, and for new hypopituitarism, without assuming postoperative recovery of hormone deficits. Surgical resection is a principal treatment for Cushing disease and acromegaly, sometimes treats prolactinomas, and is preferred for the exceedingly rare TSH-secreting adenomas, which are even less often incidental.

document_sections.heading: When is surgical resection indicated for cystic sellar incidentalomas?
document_sections.content: R32 recommends detailed MRI and hormone assessment to distinguish diagnoses for an incidental cystic sellar lesion. R33 suggests multidisciplinary discussion of surgical benefits and risks for symptomatic cystic adenomas, particularly medication-refractory severe headache or a large cystic lesion with apoplexy. R34 suggests serial pituitary MRI for asymptomatic RCCs <10 mm, with frequency guided by clinical characteristics as for adenomas. R35 suggests multidisciplinary consideration of surgery’s benefits and risks, including expert neurology input, for a small RCC <10 mm with severe headache refractory to anti-headache medication. R36 recommends surgery for an enlarging cystic lesion accompanied by visual and/or hormonal dysfunction. R37 suggests observation for arachnoid cysts <10 mm and for asymptomatic cysts ≥10 mm. R38 suggests an evidence-based multidisciplinary discussion of observation versus surgery for a stable craniopharyngioma <10 mm; expert-neurosurgeon surgery may benefit a suitable candidate through safe complete resection and pathological confirmation, whereas observation may be reasonable for a frail patient without central mass-effect findings. R39 recommends resection of enlarging and large craniopharyngiomas ≥10 mm, followed by medication and/or radiation if gross total resection is not attained; observation may be reasonable at age ≥65 years or with frailty when vision remains intact. Across cystic sellar lesions, 20% are diagnosed incidentally; others generally present with compression causing headache or visual compromise. Clinical, biochemical and imaging distinctions are important.

document_sections.heading: Rathke cleft cysts
document_sections.content: RCCs account for up to one-third of incidental pituitary lesions at autopsy and 19% of non-adenomatous MRI-detected masses. Average maximum diameter was 13 mm among 116 RCCs and ranged from 9 mm to 30 mm among 27. Imaging often shows a waxy nodule; approximately 40% have low T2-weighted and high T1-weighted signal without contrast enhancement, probably reflecting protein content. A thin wall, little enhancement, a pars intermedia location and anterior stalk displacement are common. Long-term progression affects a minority, regression occurs, and morphology has not predicted size change. Of 229 RCCs followed for a median of 36.6 months, 32% regressed spontaneously; among 110 observed for a median of 23 months, 13.6% regressed and 6.4% disappeared. Among 94 followed for a mean of 27 months, 76.5% were stable, 5% grew and 16% shrank. In a 75-person series, 21 cysts enlarged; mean calculated growth was 0.0010 cm3 per month (95% CI 0.0015–0.0035), not statistically distinguishable from zero, and only nine underwent surgery. Given slow growth, asymptomatic RCCs are usually monitored. Surgery may be considered for a cyst <10 mm with intractable headache or a lesion ≥10 mm or progressively growing with visual and/or hormonal impairment. New AVP-D occurred in 0–9% after drainage and in 19–69% after complete cyst removal. Postoperative cerebrospinal fluid leakage should be avoided; cyst closure may be needed.

document_sections.heading: Cystic pituitary adenomas
document_sections.content: Haemorrhage or ischaemic infarction can produce an MRI-visible cystic component. Reported features include variable T1-weighted signal, isointense T2-weighted signal, wall or nodular enhancement, internal septa, an eccentric location, invasion and fluid layering from earlier haemorrhage. Among 47 surgically treated patients, including 27 (57%) with RCC and 17 (36%) with cystic adenomas, amenorrhoea and/or oligomenorrhoea, reduced libido and galactorrhoea were reported in 24–47% of cystic adenomas versus 12.8–34.0% of RCCs. After cystic adenoma surgery, 70% reported headache improvement, 80% visual improvement and 33% hormonal improvement. Severe refractory headache or hormone excess may therefore lead to consideration of surgery for symptomatic lesions.

document_sections.heading: Box 3 | Future directions
document_sections.content: Research priorities include prospective follow-up for >10–15 years, particularly at ages 40–65 years; predictors of sustained growth or new hormone excess; standardized MRI reporting of lesion volume, chiasmal distance in millimetres and modified Knosp classification; and clearer distinction between adenoma and artefact for lesions <5 mm. Other proposed work concerns surveillance costs, advanced analytics, mental health effects of prolonged monitoring, management of adults <65 years old and women planning pregnancy, and approaches to incidental craniopharyngiomas <10 mm, including possible early targeted treatment for papillary disease. These are proposed research topics, not established management recommendations.

document_sections.heading: Craniopharyngiomas
document_sections.content: Craniopharyngiomas constitute 1% of intracranial tumours and 5–10% of sellar tumours in children. Adamantinomatous lesions are described as invariably cystic, often calcified and limited to the sella; papillary lesions more often look solid or mixed cystic–solid. Wall enhancement and T1-weighted hyperintensity can occur. Calcification, a normal-sized sella and a suprasellar cyst favour adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma over other cystic lesions. Post-contrast 3D T2-FLAIR can help distinguish these lesions from RCCs, whose walls enhance less often. Craniopharyngiomas may behave more aggressively than other cysts. Treatment at diagnosis or upon growth may improve outcomes, particularly below age <65 years and for papillary tumours potentially responsive to medication. Decompression can relieve mass effects; gross total resection can achieve remission, while subtotal resection plus radiation may provide comparable long-term control. Because both surgery and radiation can cause morbidity, observation until documented growth may also be reasonable.

document_sections.heading: Arachnoid cysts
document_sections.content: Arachnoid tissue herniating through a diaphragma sellae defect can form an arachnoid cyst; these represent 1.4% of sellar lesions. MRI appearance is isointense to cerebrospinal fluid without contrast enhancement. In a series of 485 identified over 10 years, 92.5% of adults and 72.4% of children were asymptomatic; after a mean of 31 months, 95% showed stable volume and no previously asymptomatic patient developed symptoms. In another series of 213 observed for 3.8 years, 5 (2.3%) enlarged and 2 (0.9%) developed new or worsening symptoms. Small cysts <10 mm and asymptomatic larger cysts ≥10 mm can therefore be managed by observation.

document_sections.heading: Special considerations
document_sections.content: The panel considered management in multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1, children and adolescents, older patients aged >65 years, and pregnant women. The available statement directs individualized decisions according to the patient and lesion, with expert multidisciplinary involvement where needed; further population-specific detail is identified as supplementary material.

document_sections.heading: Managing patient expectations
document_sections.content: Recommendations draw on peer-reviewed evidence and collective expert judgement. A patient survey was used to examine experiences with diagnosis and follow-up. Of 275 respondents, 84% were from the UK, Australia, Japan and Brazil; 46% were aged <50 years and <10% were aged ≥70 years. Sex was not recorded, and the limited sample may not represent patients in all countries. Patient communication should explain incidentaloma characteristics, evaluation, management alternatives and follow-up, emphasizing accurate specialist assessment and multidisciplinary expertise.

document_sections.heading: Conclusion
document_sections.content: An imaging-detected pituitary incidentaloma calls for careful endocrine assessment and neurosurgical or ophthalmological referral according to lesion and patient features. Diagnosis and follow-up draw on dedicated imaging, hormone testing and clinical evaluation. Decisions about NFPA surveillance versus surgery depend on patient circumstances, lesion size and location, and visual, neurological or other central mass-effect findings. Cystic lesions, lesions associated with genetic syndromes, and lesions in children, older patients or pregnant women require individualized multidisciplinary care. Prospective research is needed to establish surgical criteria for small lesions, improve decisions in difficult settings, and assess costs and mental health effects of prolonged imaging and endocrine surveillance.
